findings.message: Manual workflow_dispatch targeting production directly is broken. When environment='production' is selected, the deploy-staging job's condition evaluates false (none of the three OR branches match: not 'staging', not '', not a tag push), so staging is skipped with result 'skipped'. Then deploy-production requires needs.deploy-staging.result == 'success', which is false. The result is that no deployment occurs at all when manually dispatching to production via workflow_dispatch.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified by tracing the workflow_dispatch + environment='production' path. deploy-staging condition excludes 'production' (checks for 'staging', '', or tag), so it's skipped. deploy-production requires needs.deploy-staging.result == 'success', but skipped != success, so it also never runs. Production dispatch silently does nothing.
findings.severity_justification: An operator manually selecting 'production' deployment gets no deployment at all with no obvious error — the workflow appears to run but produces zero effect, which can delay critical releases or give a false sense of completion.
findings.category_justification: A logic error in the job conditions causes a complete control-flow failure for the production dispatch path.

findings.message: Both the blue and green compute modules create an aws_ecs_cluster with the identical name (using name_prefix which has no slot suffix). When both modules are instantiated from main.tf or providers/aws/main.tf, terraform apply will create the first cluster, then fail on the second because AWS requires unique cluster names per region. The cluster name should include var.deployment_slot (slot_name) to be unique per slot.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the ECS cluster name uses local.name_prefix (project-environment) not local.slot_name (project-environment-slot). main.tf instantiates the compute module twice (compute_blue and compute_green), each creating aws_ecs_cluster.main with identical name 'agent-monitor-production-cluster'. This causes a duplicate name conflict on apply.
findings.severity_justification: terraform apply would fail on the second cluster creation since AWS ECS cluster names must be unique per region. The entire blue-green infrastructure cannot be provisioned as written.
findings.category_justification: Logic error: the ECS cluster resource embedded in a per-slot module is instantiated twice with an identical name, making the configuration non-deployable.

findings.message: The ServiceMonitor scrapes path /api/health, which returns a JSON health response — not Prometheus text format. Prometheus will log parse errors on every scrape interval. The Helm chart defaults to /api/metrics (values.yaml line 305), so these two paths are also inconsistent. The path should be corrected to whatever Prometheus-format metrics endpoint the application actually exposes.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: servicemonitor.yaml uses path /api/health while values.yaml defaults to /api/metrics. The server only exposes /api/health which returns JSON, not Prometheus text format. Prometheus will log parse errors on every 30s scrape interval, and no metrics will be collected.
findings.severity_justification: Monitoring is broken out of the box — Prometheus will fail to parse every scrape from the Kustomize ServiceMonitor component, silently producing no metrics data. Service operation isn't impacted but observability is completely non-functional.
findings.category_justification: Wrong scrape path in the ServiceMonitor causes functional monitoring failure, and it is inconsistent with the Helm chart's default path for the same concern.

findings.message: The static scrape config for the agent-monitor job sets metrics_path: /api/health and the relabeling replaces __metrics_path__ back to /api/health. This endpoint returns a JSON health payload, not Prometheus-format metrics. Prometheus will fail to parse it and log scrape errors every 15 seconds, producing no useful metrics data.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: prometheus.yaml lines 31-32 set metrics_path: /api/health, and the server only has /api/health returning a JSON payload (not Prometheus format). Prometheus will fail to parse every scrape, generating parse errors every 15s and producing zero application metrics.
findings.severity_justification: Application-level monitoring is completely non-functional — no metrics will be collected from the app. Service operation is unaffected but observability is broken, which undermines the monitoring stack that is a key feature of this PR.
findings.category_justification: Wrong metrics endpoint path causes the Prometheus scrape job to fail on every interval, making the monitoring configuration non-functional.

findings.message: All three Trivy scanner steps pin to aquasecurity/trivy-action@master, a mutable ref. Any commit pushed to the upstream master branch will immediately affect all pipelines using this action, including potentially malicious updates. This is especially risky because this job has packages: write permission. All action references should be pinned to an immutable commit SHA.
findings.tp_fp_justification: While factually correct that aquasecurity/trivy-action@master is a mutable ref, this is a generic supply-chain best practice warning that could be copy-pasted onto any GitHub Actions workflow. It does not demonstrate a concrete exploitable vulnerability — no specific malicious commit, no demonstrated attack path. The packages:write permission concern is real in principle but is a template-level observation, not a code-specific vulnerability.
findings.severity_justification: Action pinning is a widely-known best practice but the risk is theoretical here — no concrete exploit path is demonstrated.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns software supply chain risk via a mutable action reference.

findings.message: If the first Trivy scan (app image) exits with code 1 (vulnerabilities found), the second scan step (MCP image) is skipped because it has no if: always() guard. The Upload Trivy SARIF (MCP) step does have if: always() and will run, but trivy-mcp-results.sarif was never created, causing that upload step to also fail. The net effect: when the app image has vulnerabilities, the MCP image goes unscanned.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: the MCP Trivy scan step has no if: always() guard. When the app scan exits with code 1 (vulnerabilities found), GitHub Actions skips subsequent steps without always() guards. The MCP scan is skipped, and the Upload MCP SARIF step (which has if: always()) then fails because trivy-mcp-results.sarif was never created.
findings.severity_justification: When the app image has vulnerabilities, the MCP sidecar image goes completely unscanned. A compromised or vulnerable MCP image could pass through CI undetected precisely when it matters most — when the pipeline is already flagging issues.
findings.category_justification: Logic error in step ordering/guards causes the MCP security scan to be silently skipped under a common failure condition.

findings.message: gzip -k keeps the original uncompressed file alongside the new .gz file. DB_FILENAME is updated to point to the .gz, but the original .db file is never removed. For large databases, this doubles disk consumption on the backup host with no cleanup mechanism. The -k flag should be removed so gzip replaces the original, or the original should be explicitly deleted after compression.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: gzip -k keeps the original .db file. DB_FILENAME is updated to .gz, upload_backup uses only .gz, and no code removes the original .db file anywhere in the script. Both files persist after each backup.
findings.severity_justification: Doubles disk usage for each backup but causes no data loss, correctness failure, or security issue. Impact depends on database size and backup frequency; a scheduled backup of a growing database would accumulate uncompressed copies indefinitely.
findings.category_justification: Resource management issue — leftover uncompressed files accumulate with no cleanup, potentially exhausting disk on the backup host over time.

findings.message: The Azure Files storage account primary_access_key is embedded in plain text in the azurerm_container_group resource. This key is stored unencrypted in Terraform state and propagated to the Azure container configuration API, where it can be read by anyone with access to the resource group or Terraform state. Managed identity or Key Vault secret references should be used instead.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: azurerm_storage_account.main.primary_access_key is directly embedded in the azurerm_container_group volume config at the referenced lines. This sensitive value will be stored in plaintext in Terraform state and exposed via the Azure container config API to anyone with resource group read access.
findings.severity_justification: The storage account key in Terraform state is a concrete credential exposure risk — anyone with state backend access can exfiltrate the SQLite database. Somewhat mitigated by the fact that state backend access is typically restricted, but it is a real attack surface with no secret management in place.
findings.category_justification: A concrete credential (storage account primary access key) is stored unencrypted in Terraform state and propagated plaintext to the Azure API, creating a specific data exposure risk.

findings.message: scale_down() only warns if pods do not terminate within the 120-second timeout (60 iterations × 2s), then returns normally. The restore proceeds immediately with a write to the PVC while old pods may still be running and writing to the same SQLite database. A concurrent write from a running pod against the newly-restored database can corrupt it. The function should fatal on timeout rather than warn-and-continue.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: scale_down() issues warn and returns normally on timeout. restore_database() is called immediately after regardless, mounting the PVC and overwriting dashboard.db while still-running pods may be actively writing to it, creating a concurrent write scenario on the SQLite file.
findings.severity_justification: Proceeding with a database restore while pods are still writing to the same SQLite file on the PVC can corrupt the restored database, defeating the entire purpose of the restore operation and risking data integrity.
findings.category_justification: Logic error in error handling: a timeout waiting for pod termination should abort the restore to prevent concurrent writes to SQLite, but instead the script silently continues.

findings.message: When the input file is gzip-compressed, validate_input() decompresses it with gzip -dk (keep original), sets RESTORE_FILE to the decompressed path, but never cleans it up. The decompressed file remains on disk after a successful or failed restore. For large production databases this is a significant disk leak; the restore script should trap EXIT to remove the temp file.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: gzip -dk creates a decompressed copy alongside the .gz input, RESTORE_FILE points to it, and there is no trap EXIT, cleanup function, or explicit rm of RESTORE_FILE anywhere in the script. The decompressed file leaks on both success and failure paths.
findings.severity_justification: Disk leak on the restore host for each compressed restore operation. Impact scales with database size, but this is a one-time-per-restore leak rather than an accumulating per-operation leak, and restore is an infrequent operation.
findings.category_justification: Resource management issue — temporary decompressed file is never cleaned up, leaking disk space on the operator's host.

findings.message: [yaml.github-actions.security.run-shell-injection.run-shell-injection] Using variable interpolation `${{...}}` with `github` context data in a `run:` step could allow an attacker to inject their own code into the runner. This would allow them to steal secrets and code. `github` context data can have arbitrary user input and should be treated as untrusted. Instead, use an intermediate environment variable with `env:` to store the data and use the environment variable in the `run:` script. Be sure to use double-quotes the environment variable, like this: "$ENVVAR".
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is verbatim boilerplate from a static analysis rule that could be copy-pasted onto any GitHub Actions workflow using github context in run: steps. It doesn't distinguish between the genuinely risky github.event.inputs.image_tag and the safe fixed-enum github.ref_type, and doesn't demonstrate a concrete exploit path. Triggering workflow_dispatch requires repo write access.
findings.severity_justification: The underlying concern about image_tag interpolation has some merit but exploitation requires repo write access, limiting real-world risk.
findings.category_justification: Concerns shell injection via GitHub Actions context variable interpolation in run: steps.

findings.message: [yaml.kubernetes.security.run-as-non-root.run-as-non-root] When running containers in Kubernetes, it's important to ensure that they  are properly secured to prevent privilege escalation attacks.  One potential vulnerability is when a container is allowed to run  applications as the root user, which could allow an attacker to gain  access to sensitive resources. To mitigate this risk, it's recommended to  add a `securityContext` to the container, with the parameter `runAsNonRoot`  set to `true`. This will ensure that the container runs as a non-root user,  limiting the damage that could be caused by any potential attacks. By  adding a `securityContext` to the container in your Kubernetes pod, you can  help to ensure that your containerized applications are more secure and  less vulnerable to privilege escalation attacks.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The base deployment.yaml already sets runAsNonRoot: true at both pod and container securityContext levels. The dev overlay patch is a Kustomize strategic merge patch that only overrides replicas/affinity/resources — the base securityContext is fully preserved. The static analysis tool flagged the patch file in isolation without understanding the base+overlay relationship.
findings.severity_justification: No actual security gap exists — the container runs as non-root user 1000 as defined in the base deployment that this patch applies on top of.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns container privilege escalation prevention via runAsNonRoot.

findings.message: [terraform.aws.security.aws-cloudwatch-log-group-unencrypted.aws-cloudwatch-log-group-unencrypted] By default, AWS CloudWatch Log Group is encrypted using AWS-managed keys. However, for added security, it's recommended to configure your own AWS KMS encryption key to protect your log group in CloudWatch. You can either create a new aws_kms_key resource or use the ARN of an existing key in your AWS account to do so.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verbatim boilerplate from a static analysis rule (terraform.aws.security.aws-cloudwatch-log-group-unencrypted). The finding acknowledges AWS-managed encryption is already in place and only recommends upgrading to customer-managed KMS keys — a best practice suggestion, not a concrete vulnerability. Could be copy-pasted onto any Terraform codebase lacking a kms_key_id on an aws_cloudwatch_log_group.
findings.severity_justification: Log data is already encrypted with AWS-managed keys. Customer-managed KMS is a defense-in-depth hardening measure, not a fix for an active vulnerability.
findings.category_justification: Concerns encryption key management for CloudWatch log groups.

findings.message: [terraform.aws.security.aws-efs-filesystem-encrypted-with-cmk.aws-efs-filesystem-encrypted-with-cmk] Ensure EFS filesystem is encrypted at rest using KMS CMKs. CMKs gives you control over the encryption key in terms of access and rotation.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verbatim boilerplate from a static analysis rule (terraform.aws.security.aws-efs-filesystem-encrypted-with-cmk). Recommending CMK over AWS-managed encryption is a best practice hardening suggestion, not a concrete exploitable vulnerability. Could be copy-pasted onto any Terraform EFS resource lacking an explicit kms_key_id.
findings.severity_justification: EFS encryption at rest with AWS-managed keys already provides protection. CMK is a defense-in-depth improvement for key control and rotation, not a fix for an active vulnerability.
findings.category_justification: Concerns encryption key management for EFS filesystem at rest.

findings.message: [terraform.aws.security.aws-elb-access-logs-not-enabled.aws-elb-access-logs-not-enabled] ELB has no logging. Missing logs can cause missing important event information.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The finding is verbatim boilerplate from a static analysis rule that fires on any aws_lb resource without an access_logs block. While factually correct that access logs are absent, the finding text is entirely generic and could apply to any Terraform ALB resource without change. It identifies a best-practice gap, not a concrete vulnerability.
findings.severity_justification: Missing ELB access logs reduces observability and auditability but does not create an exploitable vulnerability or affect service correctness.
findings.category_justification: Concerns audit logging and observability at the load balancer level.

findings.message: [terraform.aws.security.insecure-load-balancer-tls-version.insecure-load-balancer-tls-version] Detected an AWS load balancer with an insecure TLS version. TLS versions less than 1.2 are considered insecure because they can be broken. To fix this, set your `ssl_policy` to `"ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-Res-2021-06"`, or include a default action to redirect to HTTPS.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The HTTPS listener already uses ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06, a strong TLS 1.2+/1.3 policy. Line 136 is in the HTTP-only fallback listener (active only when TLS is not configured), which has no ssl_policy because it's plain HTTP. The finding text about 'insecure TLS version' is a mismatch for this context. Generic boilerplate that could apply to any Terraform ALB configuration.
findings.severity_justification: The HTTPS listener already enforces modern TLS. The HTTP listener is a fallback that only exists when TLS cert is not provided, which is a separate concern from TLS version selection.
findings.category_justification: Concerns TLS protocol version enforcement on an AWS load balancer.

findings.message: [terraform.aws.security.aws-subnet-has-public-ip-address.aws-subnet-has-public-ip-address] Resources in the AWS subnet are assigned a public IP address. Resources should not be exposed on the public internet, but should have access limited to consumers required for the function of your application. Set `map_public_ip_on_launch` to false so that resources are not publicly-accessible.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The flagged subnet is explicitly the public subnet tier (named aws_subnet.public) designed to host the internet-facing ALB. ECS compute tasks are placed in private subnets with assign_public_ip=false. map_public_ip_on_launch=true on public subnets is intentional and correct for this architecture. Generic boilerplate rule that doesn't understand the public/private subnet design.
findings.severity_justification: No actual exposure of compute resources — the public subnet is correctly used only for the load balancer, which must be internet-facing.
findings.category_justification: Concerns public IP assignment on AWS subnets.

findings.message: This AWS badge uses `logo=task`, which is not the correct simple-icons slug for AWS. This will render with the wrong (or no) icon. Use `amazonwebservices` (or `amazonaws`) instead.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: line 37 of README.md has `logo=task` in the AWS shield badge URL. 'task' is not the Simple Icons slug for Amazon Web Services, so the badge will render with a 'Task' icon or no recognized icon instead of the AWS logo. The same wrong logo appears in ARCHITECTURE.md. This is a concrete, verifiable error introduced by this PR.
findings.severity_justification: Cosmetic documentation issue — wrong logo renders on a badge, but has no runtime or functional impact.
findings.category_justification: The issue is in a documentation badge (shield.io image) in README.md.

'cloudways' is the Simple Icons slug for Cloudways (a managed hosting provider), not Oracle. This renders the Cloudways logo on a badge labeled 'Oracle Cloud'. The correct slug is `oracle`. Same error also in ARCHITECTURE.md. Introduced by this PR.
findings.severity_justification: Cosmetic documentation issue — wrong icon on a badge, no runtime or functional impact.
findings.category_justification: The issue is in a documentation badge in README.md.

findings.message: The MCP target group is only created and routed to here; there is no ECS service load_balancer block registering the mcp-sidecar container/port to this target group. Requests matching /mcp will therefore be forwarded to an empty target group and return 503 whenever the MCP sidecar is enabled.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: `loadbalancer/main.tf` creates `aws_lb_target_group.mcp` and listener rules routing `/mcp/*` to it, but `compute/main.tf`'s `aws_ecs_service.app` only has a single `load_balancer` block for the `app` container on `aws_lb_target_group.app`. There is no second `load_balancer` block for the MCP sidecar, and the root `main.tf` never passes the MCP target group ARN to the compute module. The MCP target group will have zero registered targets, causing 503 responses on all `/mcp/*` requests.
findings.severity_justification: When MCP sidecar is enabled, all MCP traffic routed through the load balancer will return 503 — the MCP endpoint is completely non-functional in this configuration.
findings.category_justification: Infrastructure wiring bug: a resource is created and a routing rule references it, but the compute side never registers targets to it, making the routing rule broken.

findings.message: When tls_certificate_arn is omitted, this creates an ACM certificate but never creates DNS validation records or an aws_acm_certificate_validation resource before passing the ARN to the ALB listener. The listener creation can fail or remain unusable because ACM certificates are not issued until validation completes.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: `aws_acm_certificate.main` is created with DNS validation but there are no `aws_route53_record` validation CNAME resources and no `aws_acm_certificate_validation` resource. The certificate ARN is immediately passed to the load balancer module. The certificate will stay in PENDING_VALIDATION and the HTTPS listener will be non-functional until someone manually adds DNS validation records.
findings.severity_justification: TLS is completely non-functional in any deployment that relies on the auto-provisioned ACM certificate (i.e., domain_name set but no pre-existing tls_certificate_arn). This is the expected production path and the HTTPS listener won't serve valid certificates.
findings.category_justification: Infrastructure wiring bug: a resource is created but the prerequisite validation step is never automated, leaving the configuration in a permanently broken state.

findings.message: The workflow calls npm run mcp:test, but package.json defines the MCP test script as test:mcp. This job will fail with “Missing script: mcp:test” once the workflow is run.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: package.json defines `test:mcp` (not `mcp:test`), but deployments/ci/github-actions/ci.yaml line 118 runs `npm run mcp:test`. This will fail with 'Missing script: mcp:test' every time the CI runs. The same error is also present in the GitLab CI pipeline.
findings.severity_justification: The MCP test job will always fail, breaking CI on every push/PR to main. This is a hard failure, not a warning.
findings.category_justification: CI pipeline misconfiguration that causes the test job to fail unconditionally.

findings.message: This rollback workflow is also outside .github/workflows, so it is not discoverable or executable by GitHub Actions despite declaring workflow_dispatch. Operators will not see the manual rollback action in GitHub unless the file is moved or copied into the workflows directory.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The workflow files in `deployments/ci/github-actions/` are intentionally template files. DEPLOYMENT.md line 688–689 explicitly documents the copy step (`cp -r deployments/ci/github-actions/*.yaml .github/workflows/`). The same concern applies equally to all three workflow files, and the repo already has a separate live `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. This is a deliberate template storage pattern, not an oversight.
findings.severity_justification: Even if treated as a real concern, the impact is limited to operators who skip the documented setup step; the documentation addresses it.
findings.category_justification: The finding is really about discoverability of deployment setup instructions, not a functional defect.

findings.message: The default ServiceMonitor path is /api/metrics, but the server only registers /api/health and no /api/metrics route. Enabling monitoring from the chart will scrape a nonexistent endpoint and produce no application metrics.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: `values.yaml` line 314 sets `path: /api/metrics` for the ServiceMonitor, but `server/index.js` registers no `/api/metrics` route — only `/api/health` and other application endpoints. Prometheus would scrape a nonexistent path and receive 404s, producing no application metrics.
findings.severity_justification: When monitoring is enabled via the Helm chart, observability is silently broken — no application metrics are collected and no alerts will fire. The feature exists in the chart but produces no useful output.
findings.category_justification: Misconfigured default value pointing to a non-existent server route, making the monitoring feature non-functional when enabled.

findings.message: The p99 latency analysis depends on http_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket, but the server currently emits no histogram with that name. This metric will evaluate to empty/NaN and block or fail canary promotion.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: the server has no Prometheus instrumentation (`prom-client` is not in package.json, no `/api/metrics` endpoint, no histogram or counter definitions). The `http_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket` histogram queried at lines 61–65 does not exist. The query will return NaN/empty, causing canary promotion to stall or fail erroneously.
findings.severity_justification: Canary analysis is entirely broken — all three metric queries reference non-existent data. A canary deployment would either block indefinitely or auto-fail, making the canary release strategy unusable as documented.
findings.category_justification: The canary analysis template queries metrics that the application never emits, making the entire canary strategy non-functional.

findings.message: The production tfvars file sets both domain_name and tls_certificate_arn to empty strings, but the load balancer module has checks that reject production deployments without both values. The documented `terraform apply -var-file=.../production/terraform.tfvars` therefore fails immediately unless users edit this committed file or pass overrides.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The validations are Terraform `check` blocks (not `precondition`/`postcondition` lifecycle blocks). In Terraform ≥1.5, `check` block assertions produce warnings but do not abort `terraform apply`. The finding's central claim — that 'terraform apply fails immediately' — is factually incorrect. The apply proceeds with warnings; production can still be deployed without TLS (though the HTTPS listener won't be created). The real concern (empty values in committed production tfvars) is a documentation/usability issue but not the hard failure described.
findings.severity_justification: While the apply doesn't fail, the committed production tfvars with empty TLS fields is a real operational gap — operators must remember to override before deploying. But the failure mode described is wrong.
findings.category_justification: The finding makes an incorrect factual claim about Terraform check block behavior.

findings.message: Kustomize does not substitute shell-style ${IMAGE_REGISTRY} or ${IMAGE_TAG} placeholders. The base overlays only rewrite the main app image, so enabling this component will render an invalid literal image reference for the MCP sidecar and the pod will fail to pull/start.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: `deployment-patch.yaml` line 12 uses shell-style `${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/agent-monitor-mcp:${IMAGE_TAG}`. Kustomize performs no shell variable substitution in patch files. The overlays define `images:` transformers only for the main app image, not for the MCP sidecar. Enabling the component produces a pod spec with literal `${IMAGE_REGISTRY}/agent-monitor-mcp:${IMAGE_TAG}` as the image, which is an invalid reference that will fail to pull.
findings.severity_justification: Any pod using the mcp-sidecar component will fail to start with an ImagePullBackOff error. The MCP sidecar feature is completely non-functional in the Kustomize deployment path.
findings.category_justification: Wrong use of Kustomize — shell placeholder syntax in a patch file that Kustomize never evaluates, producing an invalid pod spec.

findings.message: The MCP server reads MCP_HTTP_PORT and MCP_HTTP_HOST, but this component sets MCP_PORT and never sets MCP_HTTP_HOST. The server therefore keeps its default bind address of 127.0.0.1, while Kubernetes probes/services target the pod IP, so the sidecar will fail readiness/liveness and cannot be reached through the Service.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: `app-config.ts` uses `env.MCP_HTTP_PORT` for port and defaults `env.MCP_HTTP_HOST` to `127.0.0.1`. The HTTP server binds to `config.httpHost`. The patch sets `MCP_PORT` (wrong variable name) and omits `MCP_HTTP_HOST`, so the server binds only to `127.0.0.1`. Kubernetes `tcpSocket` readiness/liveness probes target the pod IP, not localhost, so they will fail. The sidecar also can't be reached via a Kubernetes Service.
findings.severity_justification: The MCP sidecar will perpetually fail readiness probes and never become ready in Kubernetes, making the entire mcp-sidecar component non-functional in the Kustomize deployment path.
findings.category_justification: Wrong environment variable names and missing host binding configuration cause the sidecar to bind to loopback only, breaking Kubernetes health probes and Service routing.

findings.message: The MCP sidecar configuration uses DASHBOARD_URL and MCP_PORT, but the MCP runtime reads MCP_DASHBOARD_BASE_URL, MCP_HTTP_PORT, and MCP_HTTP_HOST. Because MCP_HTTP_HOST is not set, HTTP mode binds to 127.0.0.1 by default and the Kubernetes Service/probes cannot reach the sidecar port.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: Helm values.yaml sets `DASHBOARD_URL` and `MCP_PORT` but the MCP runtime reads `MCP_DASHBOARD_BASE_URL` (app-config.ts line 88) and `MCP_HTTP_PORT`. Additionally, `MCP_HTTP_HOST` is absent, so the HTTP server defaults to binding on `127.0.0.1` (app-config.ts line 97), making the sidecar unreachable via Kubernetes probes and Services which target the pod IP.
findings.severity_justification: Same class of defect as Finding 12: the MCP sidecar deployed via Helm will bind to loopback only, fail readiness probes, and be unreachable via the Service. Additionally the dashboard base URL is misconfigured so MCP tool calls will use the wrong (default) endpoint.
findings.category_justification: Wrong environment variable names in Helm values cause the MCP sidecar to bind to loopback and use incorrect dashboard URL, making it non-functional in Kubernetes.

findings.message: azurerm_container_group.container expects environment_variables as a map argument, not repeatable nested blocks. This dynamic block is not valid for the provider schema, so Terraform validation/planning for Azure will fail before creating the container group.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: the same Azure main.tf file uses `environment_variables = { ... }` as a map at line 289 (correct for the azurerm provider schema), while lines 236–240 and 329–333 erroneously use `dynamic "environment_variables"` blocks with `name`/`value` keys. The azurerm provider's `container` block defines `environment_variables` as a `map(string)` attribute, not a nested block. Using a dynamic block on a map attribute is invalid Terraform and will fail during validate/plan.
findings.severity_justification: The Azure provider deployment path will fail immediately at terraform validate/plan, making Azure deployments completely non-functional.
findings.category_justification: Invalid Terraform HCL syntax using dynamic blocks on a map attribute instead of a simple map assignment.

findings.message: The green service only runs when active_deployment_slot is green, but the documented canary flow sets green_weight > 0 before flipping the active slot. That will route part of production traffic to a green target group with desired_count 0, causing 503s during canary/blue-green validation.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: the green compute module uses `desired_count = var.active_deployment_slot == "green" ? var.desired_replicas : 0`. The documented canary flow in production terraform.tfvars explicitly sets `green_weight = 10` before flipping `active_deployment_slot = "green"`. During this canary phase, the green target group has 0 running tasks while receiving live traffic, producing 503s for all requests routed to the green slot.
findings.severity_justification: The canary/blue-green deployment flow documented in the codebase will cause 503 errors on production traffic during the documented transition steps. The core blue-green/canary feature is functionally broken for the AWS deployment path.
findings.category_justification: Architectural mismatch: instance count is tied to the active slot variable, but traffic weighting is independent, making the documented multi-step canary flow impossible without causing partial outages.

findings.message: The root module has the same traffic-splitting problem: the green slot is scaled to zero unless it is already active, so setting green_weight for canary/blue-green testing sends traffic to an empty target group instead of warming the new slot.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed in Finding 16 investigation: root main.tf lines 106–108 set `desired_count = var.active_deployment_slot == "green" ? var.desired_replicas : 0` for compute_green. This is the same logic as in the AWS provider, and the same documented canary flow applies at the root module level. Setting green_weight > 0 before flipping active_deployment_slot routes traffic to a zero-replica green target group, producing 503s.
findings.severity_justification: Same impact as Finding 16 — the root module's canary/blue-green flow is broken for the same reason. Any deployment using the root module directly faces the same 503 issue during traffic weight transitions.
findings.category_justification: Same architectural mismatch as Finding 16: instance count tied to active slot variable while traffic weight is independent.

findings.message: This blue slot runs three replicas against the same agent-monitor-data PVC. The base PVC is ReadWriteOnce, so with the required pod anti-affinity across nodes only one replica can mount it and the rest can remain pending; the blue/green strategy needs RWX storage or per-replica claims.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: deployment-blue.yaml sets 3 replicas with `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` anti-affinity on `kubernetes.io/hostname` (pods must be on separate nodes), while base/pvc.yaml uses `accessModes: ReadWriteOnce` (only one node can mount). With pods forced to different nodes by required anti-affinity, only one replica can mount the RWO PVC; the other two will remain Pending.
findings.severity_justification: Only 1 of 3 blue slot replicas will ever become Ready; the deployment effectively runs at 1/3 capacity and the deployment will never reach its full desired state, undermining HA.
findings.category_justification: Incompatible combination of required pod anti-affinity (across nodes) and ReadWriteOnce PVC access mode, preventing multi-replica deployments from functioning.

findings.message: This green slot has the same multi-replica ReadWriteOnce PVC problem as the blue slot. With three replicas and required anti-affinity, only one node can attach the claim, so the standby slot may never become ready for a traffic switch.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: deployment-green.yaml has replicas: 3, requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution anti-affinity on kubernetes.io/hostname, and mounts the same agent-monitor-data ReadWriteOnce PVC as the blue slot. Identical to the blue slot issue — only one node can mount the RWO PVC while required anti-affinity forces pods to separate nodes, leaving 2 of 3 replicas Pending.
findings.severity_justification: The standby (green) slot cannot reach full readiness before a traffic switch, undermining the entire blue-green strategy's safety guarantee that the new slot is healthy before receiving traffic.
findings.category_justification: Same incompatible combination of required pod anti-affinity and ReadWriteOnce PVC as the blue slot finding.

findings.message: The canary deployment also mounts the same ReadWriteOnce PVC used by the stable deployment. On clusters where the stable pods are already attached on another node, the canary pod can stay pending and the rollout analysis never starts.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: canary-deployment.yaml mounts the same `agent-monitor-data` PVC (line 121) which is ReadWriteOnce per base/pvc.yaml. The canary has no affinity rules to co-locate with stable pods. On a multi-node cluster where the stable deployment already has the RWO volume attached on a node, a canary pod scheduled to a different node will be stuck Pending with a VolumeMountConflict, and the rollout analysis never starts.
findings.severity_justification: The canary deployment strategy is broken in the common multi-node cluster case — the canary pod will be stuck Pending, meaning no canary analysis runs, no traffic shifts, and no promotion or rollback occurs.
findings.category_justification: RWO PVC shared between stable and canary pods without co-location affinity, causing mount conflicts on multi-node clusters.

findings.message: This creates an FSS file system above but the container actually mounts an EMPTYDIR volume at /app/data. The SQLite database will be ephemeral and lost when the container instance is replaced, contrary to the persistent storage promised by this provider implementation.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: an `oci_file_storage_file_system` is provisioned but the container's `volumes` block uses `volume_type = "EMPTYDIR"` with `backing_store = "EPHEMERAL_STORAGE"` for `/app/data`. The code itself includes a comment acknowledging OCI Container Instances cannot mount NFS directly. The FSS is unused and the SQLite database is lost on container restart/replacement.
findings.severity_justification: All session and event data stored in SQLite is lost every time the OCI container instance is replaced or restarted. This is a silent data loss issue for any production deployment on OCI using Container Instances.
findings.category_justification: The persistent storage resource is provisioned but never connected to the container, resulting in ephemeral database storage contrary to the module's intent.

findings.message: The Kubernetes Service exposes port 80 (targetPort http/4820), but this health check port-forwards local 14820 to service port 4820. kubectl port-forward against svc/agent-monitor will fail because the Service has no port 4820, causing rollback health checks to fail even when pods are healthy.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: rollback.sh sets APP_PORT=4820 and runs `kubectl port-forward svc/agent-monitor 14820:4820`. The base Service (service.yaml) only exposes port 80 (targetPort: http/4820). kubectl port-forward against a Service requires the remote port to be a Service port (80), not a pod target port (4820). The port-forward command will fail, making the post-rollback health check always report failure regardless of actual pod health.
findings.severity_justification: Post-rollback health checks will always fail erroneously, making automated rollback verification unreliable. Operators may think a successful rollback failed, or the script may take incorrect remediation action.
findings.category_justification: Wrong port used in kubectl port-forward against a Service — the Service port (80) must be used, not the pod/container port (4820).

findings.message: The Helm and Kustomize Services expose port 80, not 4820. This port-forward targets service port 4820, so the post-rollback health check will fail with a missing service port even if the rollback succeeded.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: rollback.yaml line 104 runs `kubectl port-forward svc/agent-monitor 14820:4820`. The base Service (service.yaml) only exposes port 80 — port 4820 is not a Service port. The kubectl port-forward against a Service requires the remote port to be a defined Service port, so this command fails, making the post-rollback health check always report failure.
findings.severity_justification: Same impact as Finding 23: post-rollback health verification in the CI pipeline always fails spuriously, making the automated rollback workflow report failure even on a successful rollback.
findings.category_justification: Wrong Service port used in kubectl port-forward — same error pattern as rollback.sh.

findings.message: The Kustomize overlays and manifests hard-code namespace: agent-monitor, but the rollback script defaults to agent-monitor-<env>. Running the documented kustomize rollback without --namespace will look in the wrong namespace and report no deployment/history even when the release exists.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: all Kustomize overlays (dev/staging/production) use `namespace: agent-monitor` and base/namespace.yaml creates `agent-monitor`. The rollback.sh default namespace is `agent-monitor-${ENVIRONMENT}` (e.g. `agent-monitor-production`). Running kustomize rollback without --namespace will look in `agent-monitor-production`, find no deployment, and fail even though the release exists in `agent-monitor`.
findings.severity_justification: The documented kustomize rollback flow fails out-of-the-box without manually overriding --namespace. In an emergency, operators following the documentation will be unable to roll back.
findings.category_justification: Namespace mismatch between Kustomize manifests (agent-monitor) and the script's default namespace convention (agent-monitor-<env>).

findings.message: The MCP sidecar exposes legacy SSE endpoints at /sse and /messages (and /health), but this listener rule only forwards /mcp paths to the MCP target group. Those documented legacy MCP endpoints will be routed to the main app instead and return 404/incorrect responses.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: `http-server.ts` exposes `/mcp` (streamable), `/sse` (legacy SSE GET), `/messages` (legacy SSE POST), and `/health`. The load balancer routing rules in `loadbalancer/main.tf` only match `/mcp` and `/mcp/*`. Requests to `/sse`, `/messages`, and `/health` fall through to the main app target groups which don't handle them, returning 404.
findings.severity_justification: Legacy SSE MCP clients (which use /sse + /messages) cannot reach the MCP sidecar through the load balancer. Only the newer streamable-HTTP transport on /mcp would be routed correctly (and even that is broken per Finding 4). The documented legacy endpoints are unreachable.
findings.category_justification: Incomplete path-based routing rules miss the MCP sidecar's legacy SSE endpoints, causing those requests to be misrouted to the main application.

findings.message: Adding the MCP sidecar only opens the container port; the component does not patch the Service to add a matching mcp port. As a result, enabling the component still leaves the MCP HTTP server unreachable via the agent-monitor Service.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: the mcp-sidecar component only has deployment-patch.yaml and kustomization.yaml — no service-patch.yaml. The base Service exposes only port 80 (targetPort: http/4820). Enabling the component adds the container port 8819 to the pod spec but does not add a corresponding Service port. The MCP HTTP server remains unreachable via the agent-monitor Service.
findings.severity_justification: The MCP sidecar is unreachable through the Kubernetes Service after enabling the component, making the MCP HTTP transport completely non-functional for external clients. Direct pod-to-pod communication within the cluster would still work.
findings.category_justification: Incomplete Kustomize component — patches the Deployment but omits the required Service patch to expose the MCP port.

findings.message: Serverless NEGs for Cloud Run do not support explicit backend service health checks. Attaching google_compute_health_check.main to a backend service whose backends are SERVERLESS NEGs will be rejected by the Compute API during apply.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: the GCP backend service uses two serverless NEGs (network_endpoint_type = SERVERLESS, cloud_run backends) while simultaneously attaching a google_compute_health_check via `health_checks`. GCP's Compute API rejects health checks on backend services backed by serverless NEGs — this is a documented API constraint. The terraform apply will fail for the GCP provider.
findings.severity_justification: The GCP provider's terraform apply will be rejected by the Compute API, making the entire GCP deployment path non-functional.
findings.category_justification: Invalid GCP API configuration: health checks cannot be attached to backend services with serverless NEG backends, violating a documented Compute API constraint.

findings.message: The MCP sidecar runtime expects MCP_TRANSPORT=http plus MCP_HTTP_PORT/MCP_HTTP_HOST for HTTP mode, but this task definition only sets MCP_PORT. The sidecar will default to stdio/127.0.0.1 settings, so the ALB MCP route cannot reach an HTTP server on the task ENI.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: the ECS task definition only sets `MCP_PORT` and `NODE_ENV` for the sidecar. `app-config.ts` reads `MCP_TRANSPORT` (line 95) defaulting to `stdio` when unset (line 81). Without `MCP_TRANSPORT=http`, no HTTP server starts. Also `MCP_HTTP_PORT` is not set (wrong var `MCP_PORT` used) and `MCP_HTTP_HOST` is absent (would default to 127.0.0.1). The ALB MCP route has no HTTP endpoint to forward to on the task ENI.
findings.severity_justification: The MCP sidecar in the ECS compute module runs in stdio mode instead of HTTP mode, making the ALB's MCP routing rules non-functional. Same class of misconfiguration as Findings 12 and 13.
findings.category_justification: Missing and wrong MCP environment variables cause the sidecar to run in the wrong transport mode, preventing HTTP accessibility.

findings.message: The Azure MCP sidecar is configured with MCP_PORT only, but the MCP process reads MCP_TRANSPORT, MCP_HTTP_PORT, and MCP_HTTP_HOST. It will not start the HTTP transport on the container group's private IP, so the declared MCP port is not actually usable.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: Azure MCP sidecar environment_variables only sets `MCP_PORT` and `NODE_ENV`. As established in earlier findings, the MCP runtime reads `MCP_TRANSPORT` (defaults to stdio when absent), `MCP_HTTP_PORT` (not `MCP_PORT`), and `MCP_HTTP_HOST` (defaults to 127.0.0.1). Without `MCP_TRANSPORT=http`, no HTTP server starts on the container group's private IP, making the declared MCP port unusable.
findings.severity_justification: Same impact as Findings 12, 13, 29 — the MCP sidecar runs in stdio mode with no HTTP server, making the MCP port non-functional in the Azure deployment path.
findings.category_justification: Same missing/wrong MCP environment variables pattern as other deployment targets, causing the sidecar to start in the wrong transport mode.

findings.message: The OCI MCP sidecar has the same environment mismatch: MCP_PORT is not read by the runtime, and MCP_TRANSPORT/MCP_HTTP_HOST are missing. The container will default away from externally reachable HTTP mode, so the configured MCP port cannot serve clients.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: OCI MCP sidecar environment_variables at lines 359–362 only sets `MCP_PORT` and `NODE_ENV` — same pattern as Azure (Finding 30) and ECS compute module (Finding 29). The MCP runtime reads `MCP_TRANSPORT` (defaults to stdio), `MCP_HTTP_PORT` (not `MCP_PORT`), and `MCP_HTTP_HOST` (defaults to 127.0.0.1). Without `MCP_TRANSPORT=http` no HTTP server starts, making the configured MCP port non-functional.
findings.severity_justification: Same impact as Findings 29 and 30 — MCP sidecar runs in stdio mode with no HTTP server, making the MCP port completely non-functional in the OCI deployment path.
findings.category_justification: Same missing/wrong MCP environment variables pattern repeated for the OCI provider.

findings.message: The GCP sidecar container does not set MCP_TRANSPORT=http, MCP_HTTP_PORT, or MCP_HTTP_HOST. The MCP runtime defaults to stdio and 127.0.0.1, so this Cloud Run sidecar will not expose a reachable HTTP MCP endpoint despite declaring the sidecar image.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: GCP Cloud Run sidecar at lines 265–268 only sets `NODE_ENV=production`. No `MCP_TRANSPORT`, `MCP_HTTP_PORT`, or `MCP_HTTP_HOST` are set. As established across Findings 12, 13, 29–31, the MCP runtime defaults to stdio transport (no HTTP server) and 127.0.0.1 binding, making the declared MCP port non-functional.
findings.severity_justification: Same impact as Findings 29–31 — MCP sidecar runs in stdio mode across all four cloud providers, making the MCP HTTP endpoint non-functional everywhere.
findings.category_justification: Same missing MCP environment variables pattern repeated for the GCP Cloud Run provider.

findings.message: The analysis queries http_requests_total, but the application does not expose that metric or any /api/metrics endpoint. Canary rollouts using this template will fail analysis because Prometheus returns no usable series for the success-rate calculation.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed in Finding 9 investigation: the server has no Prometheus instrumentation — no `prom-client` dependency, no `/api/metrics` endpoint, no `http_requests_total` counter. The success-rate analysis at lines 31–35 queries a metric that doesn't exist, so Prometheus returns no series and the canary analysis fails or stalls.
findings.severity_justification: The success-rate canary metric is non-functional for the same reason as the p99-latency metric (Finding 9) — no application metrics exist. The entire canary strategy is broken.
findings.category_justification: Canary analysis references a non-existent Prometheus metric, making the success-rate check always fail or return NaN.

findings.message: The root module advertises gcp/azure/oci here, but deployments/terraform/main.tf always instantiates the AWS-only child modules (they declare aws_vpc, aws_ecs_service, aws_lb, etc.) and has no conditional provider selection. Setting this variable to anything other than aws will still plan AWS resources or fail for missing AWS provider configuration, so the public interface is misleading and broken for the non-AWS choices.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: root main.tf instantiates modules/networking, modules/compute, modules/loadbalancer, modules/database — all exclusively AWS resources (aws_vpc, aws_ecs_cluster, aws_lb, etc.) with no conditional provider selection. The `cloud_provider` variable is validated to accept aws/gcp/azure/oci but the child modules are AWS-only. Setting cloud_provider to anything other than aws still plans AWS resources, making the interface misleading.
findings.severity_justification: Users following the root module's documented interface who set cloud_provider=gcp/azure/oci will get unexpected AWS resource provisioning or provider auth failures. The public API is deceptive about multi-cloud capability.
findings.category_justification: The root module's cloud_provider variable accepts non-AWS values but unconditionally deploys AWS-only child modules, creating a broken public interface.

findings.message: The Helm defaults enable multiple replicas while the default PVC access mode is ReadWriteOnce. With the production values increasing this to three replicas and adding node anti-affinity, only one node can mount the SQLite volume and additional pods can remain unschedulable; the chart needs RWX storage or single-writer semantics before enabling multi-replica by default.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Confirmed: values.yaml sets replicaCount: 2 and accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]. values-production.yaml increases to replicaCount: 3 and adds requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution anti-affinity on kubernetes.io/hostname (pods MUST be on different nodes). With 3 replicas forced to separate nodes and a RWO PVC, only one replica can mount the volume; the others remain Pending. Same hard-constraint issue as Findings 18/19.
findings.severity_justification: Production Helm deployments will have 2 of 3 replicas stuck Pending on the PVC, rendering the multi-replica HA configuration non-functional.
findings.category_justification: Same incompatible combination of required cross-node anti-affinity and ReadWriteOnce PVC as Findings 18/19, this time in the Helm chart.

findings.message: This workflow is under deployments/ci/github-actions, but GitHub Actions only discovers workflow files in .github/workflows. As added, this CI pipeline will never run unless users manually copy it, so the promised lint/test/build/security checks are not actually wired into the repository.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Same design pattern as Finding 7: the workflow files in `deployments/ci/github-actions/` are intentionally template files documented for copying to `.github/workflows/`. DEPLOYMENT.md line 688–689 explicitly states `cp -r deployments/ci/github-actions/*.yaml .github/workflows/`. The repo already has a live `.github/workflows/ci.yml` providing CI coverage. The finding mischaracterizes deliberate template storage as a wiring omission.
findings.severity_justification: No functional impact — the existing .github/workflows/ci.yml provides active CI, and the copy step is documented for those who want to adopt the new deployment pipeline.
findings.category_justification: The finding is about discoverability of deployment setup instructions rather than a functional defect.
